points.title: Definition of a user interface
points.must: The means by which a user and a computer system communicate: how the user gives commands/data and how the system presents information and feedback.
points.model: User interface — the means by which a user and a computer system communicate: how the user gives commands and data to the system and how the system presents information and feedback to the user.

points.title: Three factors for choosing an interface
points.must: User, task and environment, each with a question to ask and an example.
points.model: User — expert or beginner, age, disabilities, language (administrator vs 7-year-old). Task — simple or complex, repetitive, precise, visual (configuring 100 servers vs browsing photos). Environment — noise, hands free/sterile, screen size (car, operating theatre, market stall).

points.title: Definition of a GUI and WIMP
points.must: GUI defined; WIMP = windows, icons, menus, pointer, each explained; interaction by pointing, clicking, dragging, tapping.
points.model: GUI — an interface based on windows, icons, menus and a pointer (WIMP) or touch, where users point, click, drag and tap visual objects instead of typing commands. Window = area showing one program/document; icon = picture standing for a file/program/action; menu = list of options to choose from; pointer = arrow moved by mouse/touchpad/finger.

points.title: Advantages of a GUI
points.must: At least four with reasons: intuitive/easy to learn (recognition not recall), fewer errors (choose from options, Undo, confirmations), WYSIWYG and visual feedback / multimedia, multitasking and drag-and-drop.
points.model: 1) Intuitive, easy to learn — users recognise icons and menus, no commands to remember; good for beginners. 2) Fewer errors — choose from options, confirmations, recycle bin, Undo. 3) WYSIWYG, visual feedback, can show images/video/charts. 4) Multitasking with several windows, drag-and-drop.

points.title: Disadvantages of a GUI
points.must: At least four with reasons: uses more memory/processing power/storage for graphics, slower for experts (many clicks), hard to automate and advanced settings hidden, accessibility limits (needs sight and precise pointing).
points.model: 1) Uses a lot of RAM, CPU and storage for graphics — wasted on a server. 2) Slower for experts — many clicks through menus, repeated for every item. 3) Hard to automate repetitive tasks; advanced settings may be hidden. 4) Depends on seeing the screen and precise pointing — hard for blind users or users with a tremor.

points.title: Worked example: GUI for a pharmacy till
points.must: Scenario linked to user, task and environment, with two advantages and one disadvantage.
points.model: Pharmacy with part-time students: GUI is easy to learn for new staff and reduces errors by offering buttons/choices (void item = undo); but needs more processing power and memory, and menus can be slow for fast workers → add barcode scanner and shortcut keys.

points.title: Definition of a CLI and parts of a command
points.must: CLI defined (typed text commands with exact syntax at a prompt, text replies); parts: prompt, command, option, arguments, with an example such as cp -r homework backup.
points.model: CLI — an interface in which the user types text commands with an exact syntax at a prompt and the system replies in text (bash, Command Prompt, PowerShell, router console). In 'admin@server:~$ cp -r homework backup': prompt = admin@server:~$, command = cp (copy), option = -r (include sub-folders), arguments = homework backup. The shell checks the syntax, runs the program, prints output or an error.

points.title: Advantages of a CLI
points.must: At least four with reasons: few resources (no GUI needed on a server), fast for experts, scripting/automation, full precise control, remote administration over SSH/slow links.
points.model: 1) Server does not need a complex OS/GUI, so no unnecessary computing resources are used. 2) Fast for experts — one line replaces many clicks. 3) Scripts automate repeated tasks (create 200 accounts from a file) without human error. 4) Full, precise control of every setting. 5) Works remotely over slow links with SSH.

points.title: Disadvantages of a CLI
points.must: At least three with reasons: commands and syntax must be learnt and remembered (not intuitive, hard to discover), typing errors can be serious with no undo, text only / unfriendly error messages.
points.model: 1) Commands, options and exact syntax must be learnt and remembered — recall, not intuitive, hard to discover what exists. 2) A typing error can make the command fail or do damage (delete a folder); often no Undo or confirmation. 3) Text only — no images/video; error messages hard for beginners to understand.

points.title: GUI vs CLI comparison
points.must: A comparison of GUI and CLI on learning, speed for experts, automation, resources, errors, control and remote use.
points.model: Learning: GUI easy / CLI hard. Expert speed: GUI slower / CLI faster. Automation: GUI difficult / CLI easy with scripts. Resources: GUI high / CLI low. Errors: GUI fewer, Undo / CLI typing errors, no Undo. Control: GUI settings hidden / CLI full control. Remote: GUI poor / CLI good (SSH).

points.title: NLI: definition and how a spoken request is processed
points.must: NLI defined (ordinary spoken or typed language, e.g. voice assistants, chatbots); stages: speech recognition → NLP finds intent and entities → action → speech synthesis.
points.model: Natural-language interface — lets users communicate in ordinary human language, spoken or typed, instead of commands or menus (Siri, Alice, chatbots, car voice control). Stages: speech recognition (sound → text) → natural-language processing finds the intent (forecast) and entities (Turkistan, tomorrow) → action performed → reply spoken by speech synthesis.

points.title: Advantages and disadvantages of an NLI
points.must: Advantages: no commands to learn, hands-free/eyes-free, accessible (blind, motor impairments), works without screen/keyboard. Disadvantages: ambiguity → misinterpretation (homophones, colloquial, context), accents/dialects/noise, may need to learn phrases, privacy, needs processing power/Internet.
points.model: Advantages: no commands to learn, many ways of asking accepted; hands-free and eyes-free (driver, cook); accessible for blind and motor-impaired users; works on devices with no screen/keyboard; quick for simple requests. Disadvantages: language is ambiguous → misinterpretation (homophones 'write/right', colloquial language, context); accents, mixing Kazakh/Russian, background noise reduce accuracy; users may need to learn phrases that work; privacy — always listening, recordings stored, others hear you; needs processing power and often the Internet.

points.title: GRI: definition and how gestures are recognised
points.must: GRI defined (detects body movements with touchscreens, cameras, depth or motion sensors); surface/air/device gestures; camera captures frames → tracks key points → matches stored patterns → command; calibration.
points.model: Gesture-recognition interface — detects movements of the body (hands, fingers, head, eyes) with touchscreens, cameras, depth sensors or motion sensors and interprets them as commands. Gestures on a surface (swipe, pinch), in the air (wave, open palm) or by moving a device (tilt, shake). Camera captures many frames per second → software tracks fingertips/joints → movement compared with stored patterns (machine learning) → command run. May need calibration for user/room/lighting.

points.title: Advantages and disadvantages of a GRI
points.must: Advantages: natural/intuitive, touchless and hygienic (surgeon, kiosk), works in noise, immersive, helps some users. Disadvantages: misinterpreted/accidental gestures, must learn gestures (differ by system and culture), limited commands and low precision, fatigue, needs sensors/space/lighting/calibration.
points.model: Advantages: natural and intuitive; touchless, so hygienic — a surgeon keeps gloves sterile; not affected by noise; immersive for games/VR; helps users who cannot type or speak. Disadvantages: gestures misinterpreted or made accidentally → unintended commands; gestures must be learnt and differ between systems and cultures; limited number of commands, less precise than a mouse; tiring ('gorilla arm'); needs cameras/sensors, space, good lighting and calibration.

points.title: Choosing an interface for a scenario
points.must: The method (user, task, environment → advantage linked to scenario → disadvantage → how reduced) with at least three scenario choices, e.g. server → CLI, driver → NLI, surgeon → GRI, elderly → touch GUI.
points.model: Method: identify user, task, environment → choose interface whose advantages fit → state a disadvantage and how it is reduced. Remote server administrator → CLI (low resources, scripts, SSH). Driver → NLI (hands on wheel, eyes on road). Surgeon → GRI (touchless, sterile). Elderly video caller → touch GUI (large icons, intuitive). Blind student → NLI + screen reader. Hospital ward: touch GUI for nurses (NLI noisy, privacy), GRI in theatre, CLI for the server.
